title: Fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for simulating atomic nuclei
authors: James Benstead, Michael Garn, Neil Gaspar, Sean Greenaway, Angus Kan, Lloyd La Ronde, Chandan Sarma, Paul Stevenson
abstract: To maximize the value of fault-tolerant quantum computers, it is essential to develop concrete applications beyond well-established domains such as chemistry and condensed-matter physics. Here we construct and compile quantum algorithms to simulate the structure of atomic nuclei -- a topic that has received relatively little attention from the quantum computing community despite its similarities to the electronic structure problem in chemistry -- via effective shell-model Hamiltonians and no-core-shell-model Hamiltonians with three-body interactions derived from chiral effective field theory. Furthermore, we provide quantum resource estimates, in terms of Toffoli gate and qubit counts, for these algorithms, which, to our knowledge, are the first such estimates for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of atomic nuclei. Notably, the estimates for $^{32}$Mg and $^{219}$At shell-model Hamiltonians are comparable to recent estimates of Femoco simulations, a standard benchmark in chemistry. For no-core-shell-model Hamiltonians suitable for light nuclei (up to $^{40}$Ca or so), we find that resource requirements are significantly higher, suggesting that more bespoke strategies are required to make such simulations practicable. Throughout this work, we draw upon the similarities between nuclear and electronic structure problems, while also highlighting challenges that are specific to the former. We hope this work will spur long-term collaborations between the nuclear and quantum computing community with the ultimate goal of realizing useful nuclear simulations on quantum computers.
summary: This paper develops and analyzes fault-tolerant quantum algorithms designed to simulate the complex Hamiltonians governing atomic nuclei. By providing resource estimates for both effective shell-model and no-core models, it establishes a crucial benchmark for applying quantum computing to nuclear physics. The research highlights the computational challenges specific to nuclear interactions compared to electronic structure problems.
main_problem: To develop concrete applications for fault-tolerant quantum computers by simulating the complex structure of atomic nuclei.
main_result: The authors provide resource estimates for simulating nuclear Hamiltonians using both effective shell-model and no-core-shell-model approaches, noting that while some benchmarks are comparable to chemistry simulations, the full no-core model requires significantly higher resources.
method: They construct quantum algorithms based on Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) tailored for fermionic systems, utilizing techniques like Jordan-Wigner transformations and circuit optimization to estimate resource costs in terms of Toffoli gates and qubits.
model_or_system: The system is the atomic nucleus, modeled by Hamiltonians derived from chiral effective field theory. These Hamiltonians include one-, two-, and three-body interactions, which are more complex than those typically used for electronic structure problems.
key_observables: Ground state energy estimation, quantum resource estimates (Toffoli gate count, qubit counts), and nuclear structure properties.
important_parameters: The complexity scales with the number of particles and orbitals; specific parameters include $e_{\max} = 8$, $e_{2\max} = 16$, and $e_{3\max} = 8$ for EFT interactions.
main_assumptions: They assume that quantum resource estimation is the primary goal, and they compare results across different Hamiltonian formulations (phenomenological vs. no-core).
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares resource estimates for simulating the full Hamiltonian versus partitioning it by symmetry sectors ($T_z$ or $M$), showing that sector-wise simulation leads to redundancy and increased cost for no-core models.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the need for new applications beyond chemistry, detailing the construction of quantum algorithms (QPE) for nuclear Hamiltonians, providing resource estimates for specific nuclei ($^{32}	ext{Mg}$, $^{219}	ext{At}$), and finally analyzing the efficiency of Hamiltonian decomposition strategies.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the feasibility frontier of applying quantum computation to fundamental physics problems outside chemistry, offering concrete benchmarks that guide future hardware development for nuclear structure theory.
